food.text: Chinese imperial cuisine is said to have originated around the Zhou dynasty, from the 11th century to 476 BCE. Emperors used their power to collect the best cuisines and the best cooks from throughout the country. For that reason, Chinese people saw imperial cuisine as a dynasty's best cuisine.

During Shi Huangdi's Qin dynasty, the empire expanded into the south. By the time of the Han dynasty, major canals linked the different regions and the cuisines of China's peoples. This led to greater complexity in the regional cuisines.

Chinese food philosophy was rooted in the I Ching and traditional medicine. Food was thought to give "qi", or energy, and to maintain yin and yang. It was judged for color, aroma, taste and texture, and a good meal balanced the Four Natures and the Five Tastes.

Nobles hunted various wild game and ate mutton, pork and dog, because those animals had been domesticated. The flavor of meat was enhanced by cooking it in animal fats, though this practice was mostly restricted to the wealthy.

Grain was stored against famine and flood, and meat was preserved with salt, vinegar, curing and fermenting. Grains were typically served as warm noodle soups rather than baked into bread as in Europe.
Salt was used as a preservative from early times. In cooking, however, it was added in the form of soy sauce, and not at the table.

A restaurant in Xi'an has tried to bring back the cooking of Qin and Han imperial kitchens. The Qujiangchun Restaurant restored more than a dozen dishes of the Qin and Han dynasties, working from records in ancient Chinese texts.

art.text: Han dynasty tombs held clay models of buildings, made as funerary items. Because most ancient Chinese wooden architecture has vanished, with only ruins of brick and rammed earth walls and towers surviving from before the 6th century AD, these little models let scholars discern how such buildings looked.

A fundamental achievement of Chinese wooden architecture is the load-bearing timber frame, a network of interlocking wooden supports forming a building's skeleton. It is considered China's major contribution to worldwide architectural technology. Yet it is not known how the builders got the huge wooden support columns into position.

A bronze rhinoceros wine vessel from the Western Han dynasty was discovered in Shaanxi in 1963. Complex cloud patterns are inlaid into its skin with gold and silver wire. It is so lifelike that it must have been modelled on an actual rhinoceros.

Jade has been prominent in Chinese art since prehistoric times, and the highest quality jade has at times been esteemed more highly than gold, diamonds or pearls. Early jade carvings included circular disks known as bi, generally understood to represent the heavens in some fashion.

The Han-era scholar Xu Shen, by 206 BC, listed the Five Virtues of Jade as benevolence, honesty, wisdom, integrity and bravery. Jade was thus valued for moral qualities as well as beauty. By 3000 BC it was already referred to as yu.

Depictions of rhinoceroses in ancient Chinese art are typically very accurate and lifelike. This suggests artists modelled them first-hand on living animals rather than on legend or traveller's tales. Such realism points to rhinoceroses living in ancient China.

The oracle bone script and bronzeware script glyphs for elephant were pictographic depictions of an animal with a long trunk. Their modern descendant is the regular script character 象, pronounced xiàng.

The Han dynasty saw the first two forms of Chinese paper art, paper cutting and paper folding, together with the hand fan and the pinwheel. Paper cutting is attributed to Cai Lun during the Han dynasty.

The rhinoceros vessel's saddle-shaped lid is held on by straps that go around the animal's belly. This suggests the artist's model was a tame rhinoceros. Its two horns and distinctive wrinkles around the eyes are characteristic features of the Sumatran rhinoceros.

Ritual bronzes from the Shang and Zhou dynasties all depicted elephants with two fingers on the tip of the trunk. A 2011 study of these bronzes and of molars and tusks suggested the ancient Chinese elephant probably belonged to the genus Palaeoloxodon, not a subspecies of the Asian elephant.

Chinese architecture used the Great Wall as an early showcase of rammed-earth building. Hangtu, the pounding of layers of earth to make walls, altars and foundations, remained a feature of Chinese construction for millennia. The Great Wall was erected beginning in the first millennium BC.

A wooden sculpture of a charging bull-like creature with a huge single horn was discovered in 1959 in a late Western Han tomb at Wuwei, Gansu. It resembles reconstructions of Elasmotherium, and it has been speculated that the Chinese unicorn, the qilin, is a folk memory of that animal.

war.text: Chinese war chariots were used on open plains from around 1200 BCE. They gave commanders a mobile platform to control troops and let archers and soldiers with dagger-axes move faster. They peaked in importance in the Spring and Autumn period, but cavalry largely replaced them under the Han dynasty.

At the Battle of Muye in 1046 BCE, the Zhou army's infantry and chariots were ordered to stop and regroup after every six or seven steps to keep formation. The Shang army had superior numbers but was largely made up of demoralized, forcibly conscripted troops. They failed to hold formation and were defeated.

The Art of War, attributed to the strategist Sun Tzu, is a military treatise of 13 chapters from the late Spring and Autumn period. It covers weapons, logistics, morale, rank and discipline. Sun portrays war as a costly, destructive last resort, saying prolonged warfare erodes the state faster than the enemy ever could.

The Warring States period, c. 475 to 221 BC, was named partly for how the scale of warfare exploded. Chariots gave way to massed infantry with swords and crossbows, battles lasted months or even years, and iron and cavalry came into use. Reported figures include 100,000 killed at the Battle of Maling, 240,000 at the Battle of Yique, and 890,000 enemy deaths credited to General Bai Qi over his career, though scholars such as Michael Loewe and Edward L. Shaughnessy think these numbers are exaggerated. The period ended when Qin annexed every other contender state and founded the first imperial dynasty.

Against the Xiongnu at the Battle of Mobei, General Wei Qing met the Chanyu's army of 80,000 cavalry. He ordered his troops to arrange heavy-armored chariots in a ring, creating mobile fortresses. Chariots had otherwise become mostly command posts by the Han era.

The state of Chu used elephants in war in 506 BC against Wu. Torches were tied to the animals' tails and they were sent into the enemy ranks, but the attempt failed. It was one of the few times Chinese states used war elephants.

By about 300 BCE only seven main states remained: Chu, Han, Qi, Qin, Yan, Wei and Zhao. Some built rammed earth walls along their frontiers to guard against each other and against raids by nomadic tribes like the Quanrong and Xiongnu. Qin conquered the states of Ba and Shu by 316 BCE.

By the Spring and Autumn period, chariot design had improved. The curved draw pole rose at a greater angle, which cut the horse's effort and raised speed. The carriage body widened to around 1.5 m, and the pole, hubcap and yoke were reinforced with decorated copper castings.

In 1972, the Yinqueshan Han slips were found in two Han tombs near Linyi in Shandong, sealed between 134 and 118 BCE. They contained a text matching The Art of War and a separate one attributed to Sun Bin. This showed that two texts could have been called "Master Sun's Art of War", explaining long-standing confusion.

In 318 BC, Qi and Chu attacked Qin on behalf of Wei, helped by Han, Zhao and Yan. Disputes over who would lead the campaign followed a failed attack at the Hangu Pass, which let Qin take even more land. Qin later invaded Zhou and ended its line of monarchs in 256 BC.

literature.text: The Classic of Poetry is the oldest existing collection of Chinese poetry, made up of 305 works dating from the 11th to 7th centuries BC. Scholars in China and neighboring countries have studied and memorized it for over two millennia. It is also a rich source of chengyu, four-character idioms still used today.

The Chu Ci, or Songs of Chu, contrasts with the Classic of Poetry by emphasizing lyric and romantic features and irregular line lengths. It consists primarily of poems ascribed to Qu Yuan (329–299 BCE) and his follower Song Yu. In its present form it dates to Wang Yi's compilation and notes of 158 CE.

According to Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, after Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC, his chancellor Li Si suggested suppressing intellectual discourse, and the Qin is alleged to have destroyed the philosophical treatises of the Hundred Schools of Thought. Li Si viewed poetry, history and philosophy as the most politically dangerous books, believing that stories of ancient virtuous rulers would make people dissatisfied with the present. This became the legend of the "burning of books and burying of scholars", but modern historians doubt the details, which first appeared more than a century later. Michael Nylan suggests the story may rest on the razing of the Qin palace in 207 BC, when many books were undoubtedly lost.

Tradition held that Confucius edited the Classic of Poetry down from a larger collection of 3,000 pieces to the 305 we know. This claim is now generally discredited, because the Zuo Zhuan records that the Poetry already existed in a definitive form when Confucius was just a young child.

In 26 BCE, at the emperor's command, Liu Xiang compiled the first catalogue of the imperial library, called the Abstracts. He is also the first known editor of the Classic of Mountains and Seas and edited the Biographies of Exemplary Women. He was also a poet, credited with the Nine Laments in the Chu Ci.

The earliest known narrative history of China was the Zuo Zhuan, compiled no later than 389 BC and attributed to the blind 5th-century BC historian Zuo Qiuming. The Book of Documents was certainly compiled by the 4th century BC, the latest date for the Guodian Chu Slips unearthed in a Hubei tomb in 1993.

Gushi, meaning old poetry, uses uniform lines of 5 or 7 syllables arranged in syntactically paired couplets. These poems first really began to emerge as a poetic form in the second century CE. The style later enjoyed a great revival in the Tang dynasty.

The Mao Tradition of the Poetry, attributed to an obscure scholar named Mao Heng, was not officially recognized until the reign of Emperor Ping. During the Eastern Han it gradually became the primary version of the Poetry. Zheng Xuan based his 2nd-century annotated edition on it, and it later became the imperially authorized text in 653 CE.

During the Han dynasty, the Chu Ci style contributed to the evolution of the fu, a descriptive poem mixing verse and prose passages. Fu were often used as a virtuoso display of the poet's skills and knowledge rather than to convey intimate emotion. The form became shorter and more personal in the Six Dynasties period.

The oldest extant dictionary in China is the Erya, dated to the 3rd century BC and written anonymously. Later dictionaries included the Fangyan by Yang Xiong (53 BC – 18 AD) and the Shuowen Jiezi by Xu Shen (58–147 AD). Guo Pu (276–324) added commentary to the Erya.

In 2015, Anhui University purchased a group of looted manuscripts dating to about 330 BC, from the Warring States period. Among them is one of the oldest extant scribal copies of at least part of the Classic of Poetry.
The Bamboo Annals were found in 281 AD in the tomb of the King of Wei, who was interred in 296 BC. Unlike the Zuo Zhuan, however, the authenticity of the early date of the Bamboo Annals is in doubt.

science.text: Chinese star names appear on oracle bones unearthed at Anyang, dating back to the mid-Shang dynasty, around 1300 BCE. The core of the 'mansion' system for organizing the sky also took shape around this period, by the time of King Wu Ding (1250-1192 BCE).

Around AD 105, Cai Lun, an official at the Han imperial court, is traditionally credited with making a sheet of paper from mulberry and other bast fibres, fishing net, old rags, and hemp waste. Before paper, Chinese writers used pottery, bones, stones, bronzes, bamboo or wooden strips, and silk, which were too heavy or too expensive for widespread use.

Chinese astronomers recorded 1,600 observations of solar and lunar eclipses from 750 BCE. Joseph Needham described the ancient Chinese as the most persistent and accurate observers of celestial phenomena anywhere in the world before the Islamic astronomers.

The armillary sphere was built up in stages by Han astronomers. Geng Shouchang added a fixed equatorial ring in 52 BCE, and Fu An and Jia Kui added an elliptical ring by 84 CE. Zhang Heng completed the sphere in 125 CE with horizon and meridian rings.

The astronomer Shi Shen, active in the fourth century BCE, understood the relation of the Moon to a solar eclipse. His writing gave instructions for predicting eclipses from the relative positions of the Moon and the Sun.

The Book of Silk, written around 400 BC, was the first definitive atlas of comets. It listed 29 comets, called 'sweeping stars', that appeared over about 300 years, with drawings of comets describing the events their appearances corresponded to.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in China

science.text: The earliest archaeological evidence for glass manufacture in China comes from the Warring States period. Chinese glass from the Warring States period and Han dynasty contained high levels of barium oxide and lead, which distinguished it from the soda-lime-silica glass of Western Asia and Mesopotamia.
Zhang Heng, who lived from 78 to 139 CE, created the world's first hydraulic, or water-powered, armillary sphere. He operated it with an inflow clepsydra clock.

Sima Qian's star catalogue in his 'Book of Celestial Offices' featured 90 constellations and became the model for all later Chinese star catalogues. In 120 AD, Zhang Heng published a catalogue that featured 124 constellations.

The odometer cart was most likely invented in Western Han China by Luoxia Hong around 110 BC. The Greeks are thought to have invented it separately, either Archimedes in the 3rd century BC or Hero of Alexandria in the 1st century AD.

The compass's origins may be traced to the Warring States period, which used a lodestone compass called the 'south-governor' (sinan). Much later, Shen Kuo mentioned the first suspended magnetic needle compass in 1088.

Lacquerware from the 433 BC Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng carries lists of stars along the ecliptic in the Chinese Twenty-Eight Mansions. The Mawangdui Silk Texts, buried in a Western Han tomb in 168 BC, include star maps showing Chinese constellations as well as comets.

politics.text: The earliest confirmed historical period in China begins with the Shang dynasty (c. 1250 BC), which left the oldest surviving oracle bone inscriptions. It was followed by the Zhou dynasty (c. 1046 to 256 BC), an era that introduced the Mandate of Heaven.

In 221 BC, China was unified under an emperor for the first time. The Qin's wars of unification brought most of the Huaxia realm into one single dynasty, ending the Warring States period that had begun as a loose collection of Han Chinese-speaking entities.

The Zhou dynasty lasted 790 years, from c. 1046 BC until 256 BC, the longest span of any dynasty in Chinese history. During the Western Zhou period, the royal house, surnamed Ji, held military control over territories centered on the Wei River valley and North China Plain.

After the Battle of Muye, the Shang dynasty was overthrown by Zhou, led by Ji Fa. Zhou had emerged as a western state along the Wei River and shared the language and culture of the Shang people. Its kings' power fragmented not long afterwards, and many autonomous vassal states emerged.

The Eastern Zhou period (771 to 256 BC) was marked by an accelerating collapse of royal authority. Even so, the king's ritual importance enabled more than five additional centuries of rule. The Confucian chronicle called the Spring and Autumn Annals gave the early part of this period its name.

Emperor Wu dispatched a series of military campaigns against the Baiyue tribes. The Han annexed Minyue in 135 BC and 111 BC, Nanyue in 111 BC, and Dian in 109 BC. Migration and military expeditions led to the cultural assimilation of the south.

Emperor Guangwu reinstated the Han dynasty with the support of landholding and merchant families at Luoyang, east of the former capital Xi'an. Because of this, the new era is termed the Eastern Han dynasty. Under the capable administrations of Emperors Ming and Zhang, the dynasty's former glories were reclaimed.

The diplomat and general Ban Chao expanded the Han conquests across the Pamirs to the shores of the Caspian Sea. This reopened the Silk Road, bringing trade, foreign cultures, and the arrival of Buddhism. The Xiongnu Empire had also been decisively defeated.

After Wang Mang's regime ended, the monetary system stayed disrupted. Cloth, silk and grain supplemented coins as money. Cash still measured wealth in large amounts, such as one million cash gifted to Yang Ping.

In 403 BC, the Zhou court recognized Han, Zhao, and Wei as fully independent states. In 344 BC, Duke Hui of Wei was the first to claim the title of king for himself. Others followed, and rulers stopped pretending to be vassals of the Zhou court.

In 97 AD, the Chinese general Ban Chao tried to send his envoy Gan Ying to Rome. The Parthians, who wanted to keep control of the lucrative silk trade, dissuaded Gan from venturing beyond the Persian Gulf.

According to Chinese chronicles, the Kushans requested, but were denied, a Han princess, even though they had sent presents to the Chinese court. In retaliation, they marched on Ban Chao in AD 90 with a force of 70,000 but were defeated by the smaller Chinese force.

After Sima Yan founded the Jin dynasty in 265 CE, reductions in coin weights in the south caused great price fluctuations. Cloth and grain were used as substitutes for coins. Grain thus served as a stand-in for money in the Eastern Jin south.

In 256 BC, Qin captured the Zhou capital Wangcheng and killed King Nan, the last Zhou king by tradition. After Chengzhou fell to Qin forces, nobles of the Ji family proclaimed Duke Hui of Eastern Zhou as King Nan's successor. Ji Zhao, a son of King Nan, led a resistance against Qin for five years. The dukedom was fully disassembled by 249 BC.

philosophy.text: Chinese philosophy began in earnest during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, c. 770–221 BCE, an era later called the Hundred Schools of Thought. Thinkers such as Confucius, Mencius, Laozi, Zhuangzi, Mozi, Han Fei and Xunzi laid the foundations of Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism and Legalism.

Wuxing, often translated as the Five Phases or Five Elements, is a fivefold scheme used to explain phenomena across Chinese medicine, politics, religion and social relationships. It was in use earlier but was formulated in the second or first century BCE during the Han dynasty. It served as a metaphysics based on cosmic analogy.

Buddhism was introduced to China in the 1st century CE and diversified into new forms. Starting in the 3rd century CE, the school of Xuanxue emerged, interpreting earlier Daoist works with a special emphasis on metaphysical explanations.

Chinese philosophy is the dominant philosophical thought in China and in other East Asian countries that share a common language, including Japan and Korea. The Hundred Schools of Thought flourished from the 6th century to 221 BCE, a period the article says was fraught with chaos and bloody battles, yet also a Golden Age in which a broad range of ideas was freely discussed. The era ended with the rise of the Qin dynasty and the subsequent purge of dissent, and its ideas have profoundly influenced lifestyles and social consciousness in East Asia up to the present day.

Legalism's main motto was "Set clear strict laws, or deliver harsh punishment." Under the Qin dynasty it was the official philosophy, and the Qin quashed the Mohist and Confucianist schools and was blamed for creating a totalitarian society. Legalism as a coherent philosophy largely disappeared because of its tie to the unpopular authoritarian rule of Qin Shi Huang. Even so, many of its ideas and institutions kept influencing Chinese philosophy throughout the Han dynasty and after.

Legalists generally saw most people, or at least the elite, as fundamentally self-interested. They stressed equality under the law, administrative methods and regulations, strengthening agriculture and the military, and favored meritocracy over aristocratic power. This pragmatic, results-driven view put them at odds with Confucians, who relied on cultivated virtue, and with Mohists, who promoted universal love.

Zajia, the Mixed School, combined elements of Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism and Legalism. Its texts include the Shizi (c. 330 BCE), the Lüshi Chunqiu and the Huainanzi. No school actually called itself Zajia; the label was applied later, in the Han-era bibliographic catalogue.

The Qin and especially the Han dynasty inherited the philosophy of the Warring States period and molded it into a universalistic philosophy, cosmology and religion. Han philosophers stressed the crucial role of human beings on earth, completing a cosmological trinity of Heaven, Earth and humanity.

Han Fei, considered by many the greatest Legalist thinker, was strongly influenced by Daoism. He drew on the Daoist idea of wu wei, or non-action, to describe an ideal ruler who stepped back from actively managing the state and instead set universal rules and standards.

The word wuxing combines the characters for "five" and "moving". "Moving" is shorthand for planets, since the Chinese word for planets means "moving stars". The scheme originally referred to the five classical planets, which with the Sun and Moon were thought to create the forces of earthly life.

Buddhism had little impact on China until the 4th century, when its teachings hybridized with those of Taoism. It brought the idea of many hells where sinners went, though their souls could be saved by pious acts. Because Chinese thought focused on ethics rather than metaphysics, the merger produced schools distinct from the Indian originals.

Some of the Mawangdui Silk Texts, dated to before 168 BCE, connect the wuxing to the wude, the Five Virtues and Five Emotions. Scholars believe several predecessors of the wuxing concept were merged into a single system during the Han dynasty.

culture.text: Shang kings worshiped their royal ancestors as unseen divine forces after death. The ancestors were called dì, and the utmost progenitor was Shangdi, the 'highest deity'. This ancestor-centered faith shaped later Chinese religion.

Human sacrifice was a significant part of ancient Chinese culture, especially during the Shang dynasty, where the Shang king would demonstrate devotion to the supreme deity through the spectacular spilling of sacrificial human blood. Such rituals were often carried out simply as spectacles for those high in power and influence. Rulers used the phrase "The great national concerns are sacrifice and war", which historian Xinxu Liu calls a "status symbol for rulers".
culture.source_title: Human sacrifice in ancient Chinese culture

culture.text: In Chinese mythology, the goddess Nüwa mended the Heavens after a disaster destroyed the pillars holding up the skies. She used five colored stones in the five auspicious colors, which explains the many colors the skies can take.

The Zhou period saw a great cultural and philosophical diversification known as the Hundred Schools of Thought. Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism are among the most important philosophies that survive from this era.

The Zhou violently overthrew the Shang in 1046 BC, but many Shang customs persevered despite attempts at erasure. The poem "Huang Niao", or "Yellow Bird", was created to protest human sacrifice and is presumed to have been written by civilians.
culture.source_title: Human sacrifice in ancient Chinese culture

culture.text: Traditionally, China's cardinal colors were cyan, red, yellow, white and black. They corresponded to wood, fire, earth, metal and water, the five elements. Emperors of the Shang, Tang, Zhou and Qin used the Theory of the Five Elements to select colors, and Confucius considered other colors "inferior".

Confucianism grew out of the Hundred Schools of Thought from the teachings of Confucius (551-479 BCE), who saw himself as a retransmitter of Zhou golden age values. In the Han dynasty, Confucian approaches edged out the proto-Taoist Huang-Lao as the official ideology.

Whether sacrifice was ever strictly outlawed is debatable. Some sources suggest the Zhou rulers strongly condemned it, but other evidence shows rulers such as Duke Xian of Qin having people killed for religious ceremonies.
culture.source_title: Human sacrifice in ancient Chinese culture

culture.text: Ancient Chinese bronzes are celebrated for their artistic value and casting technology, and many surviving pieces are vessels. One example used for sacrifice is the Houmuwu ding, whose rectangular body bears taotie markings.
culture.source_title: Human sacrifice in ancient Chinese culture

culture.text: In the first half of 3 BCE, the earliest recorded mass religious movement in China arose, driven by belief in the imminent arrival of the Queen Mother of the West. It spread through Henan, Hebei and Shandong, and the government did not crush it.

Zhou ritual worship included ceremonies led by officials that used "bitter herb" drinks, called tu. The herb was thought an exotic plant from southern China, offered as tribute to the emperor and served to nobles. Scholars still debate whether tu was actually tea.

The Han Chinese trace their culture to the Huaxia, a confederation of agricultural tribes along the Yellow River. Qin and Han migration waves carried this culture south, and the word "Han" in the Classic of Poetry originally meant the Milky Way.

In the first half of 3 BCE, the earliest record of a mass religious movement shows excitement over the expected arrival of the Queen Mother of the West in Henan, Hebei and Shandong. The government did not crush it. Elites connected it to abnormal cosmic phenomena seen as signs of an excess of yin.
